strings.atlas.feature.1296.label: Copernicus
strings.atlas.feature.1296.naming: Copernicus honors the Polish astronomer whose Sun-centered model treated Earth as a planet. Riccioli chose the name for his 1651 Moon map even though he rejected that moving-Earth model. His map preserved the names of scholars on different sides of the debate.
strings.atlas.feature.1296.observation: Copernicus spreads bright rays across dark plains, creating a strong contrast. Near the boundary between lunar day and night, shadows reveal the crater’s shape more clearly than its rays do.
strings.atlas.feature.1296.story: In November 1966, Lunar Orbiter 2 photographed Copernicus obliquely from an altitude of about 45 kilometers. The view made its mountains and crater walls look startlingly three-dimensional. News reports celebrated it as one of the great pictures of the century.
strings.atlas.feature.2990.label: Kepler
strings.atlas.feature.2990.naming: Riccioli named this crater for German astronomer Johannes Kepler in 1651. Kepler’s three laws describe planetary motion. He worked through Tycho’s observations of Mars for years before finding that an elliptical orbit fit the data. The planets could follow a precise mathematical rule without moving in perfect circles.
strings.atlas.feature.2990.observation: West of Copernicus, Kepler is only about 30 kilometers across. In an ordinary lunar photograph, its bright surroundings and rays are easier to pick out than details inside the crater.
strings.atlas.feature.2990.story: Kepler’s central peak is off-center and irregular. The LROC team suggests this may reflect the crater’s size, near the transition between a simple bowl and a more complex crater. Orbital close-ups also reveal boulders and small impact craters on the peak.
strings.atlas.feature.3665.label: Mare Australe
strings.atlas.feature.3665.naming: The “Southern Sea” is a nineteenth-century addition to the lunar map. Wilhelm Beer and Johann Heinrich Mädler introduced the name in their 1837 book Der Mond. They argued that this inconspicuous region deserved recognition as a sea in its own right. The IAU adopted the name in 1935, almost a century after its introduction.
strings.atlas.feature.3665.observation: Australe straddles the southeastern boundary between the near and far sides. Seen from Earth, it is strongly foreshortened, and lunar libration changes how much is visible. It will not be identifiable in every photograph.
strings.atlas.feature.3665.story: Australe is a collection of dark patches separated by brighter terrain. Our view from Earth skims across the Moon’s edge, and libration, the Moon’s apparent rocking, changes how much is visible. Beer and Mädler already described how that changing view could turn a recognizable sea into scattered spots.
strings.atlas.feature.3670.label: Mare Cognitum
strings.atlas.feature.3670.naming: Mare Cognitum means “the sea that has become known.” After Ranger 7 photographed this region in 1964, astronomer Gerard Kuiper proposed two names to the IAU: Mare Exploratum and Mare Cognitum. The latter was chosen to commemorate the new close-up view of the ground. Its name records a specific step in humanity’s exploration of the Moon.
strings.atlas.feature.3670.observation: South of Insularum and northwest of Nubium, Cognitum connects with the surrounding dark plains. Its boundary is subtle, so neighboring maria are useful guides.
strings.atlas.feature.3670.story: Ranger 7 took its pictures on the way to a deliberate impact. During its final 17 minutes, it sent back 4,308 images. Imaging continued until about 0.2 seconds before impact, revealing details roughly half a meter across. The photographs helped scientists prepare for the soft landings that would follow.
strings.atlas.feature.3671.label: Mare Crisium
strings.atlas.feature.3671.naming: Crisium gives this feature the name “Sea of Crises.” Riccioli placed it on Grimaldi’s map in 1651. The name itself is well documented, but the sources here do not establish a particular crisis that inspired it. The International Astronomical Union formally adopted the existing name in 1935.
strings.atlas.feature.3671.observation: Near the Moon’s eastern edge, Crisium appears as an isolated dark oval surrounded by bright highlands. Its separation from the other large maria makes it a useful landmark.
strings.atlas.feature.3671.story: Luna 24 returned samples from Crisium in 1976, allowing laboratory measurements of the rocks’ ages. The plain also has wrinkle ridges: when the ground is compressed, it bends and fractures. Their ridged outlines preserve evidence of deformation within an apparently smooth lunar sea.
strings.atlas.feature.3673.label: Mare Fecunditatis
strings.atlas.feature.3673.naming: Fecunditatis means fecundity or fertility. Riccioli put the name on his 1651 lunar map. Alongside Serenity and Tranquility, it belongs to the more auspicious names in the eastern part of his map, reflecting an era when lunar names drew on ideas about life and human affairs.
strings.atlas.feature.3673.observation: South of Crisium and east of Tranquillitatis, Fecunditatis is a dark area with an uneven boundary. Its position toward the eastern limb makes its outline appear compressed by perspective.
strings.atlas.feature.3673.story: In September 1970, Luna 16 landed here, sampled the surface and brought about 101 grams back to Earth. It was the first robotic lunar sample return. The sampling took place after sunset, entirely in darkness: this small load of soil arrived without an astronaut collecting it.
strings.atlas.feature.3674.label: Mare Frigoris
strings.atlas.feature.3674.naming: Mare Frigoris means “Sea of Cold,” the name Riccioli published in 1651. His naming table also preserves an earlier choice by Michael van Langren: Mare Astronomicum, the “Sea of Astronomy.” The competing names let us glimpse a time when different mapmakers each proposed their own lunar geography.
strings.atlas.feature.3674.observation: North of Imbrium, Frigoris stretches sideways as a narrow dark band. Its long, irregular shape contrasts with the broad rounded outlines of Imbrium and Serenitatis.
strings.atlas.feature.3674.story: Frigoris preserves signs of surprisingly recent movement. A 2019 study of orbital images found ridges that may have moved within the past 40 million years. Their shapes and relationships with surrounding terrain help geologists distinguish younger deformation from much older structures.
strings.atlas.feature.3677.label: Mare Humorum
strings.atlas.feature.3677.naming: Today’s official gazetteer translates Humorum as “Sea of Moisture.” Riccioli used the name in 1651. Historians also relate it to the old medical idea of bodily humours, when people linked the Moon with health as well as weather. The Latin name carries that older cultural association.
strings.atlas.feature.3677.observation: West of Nubium, Humorum has a rounded dark interior with a distinct bright border. In a sufficiently clear image, Gassendi crater on the northern edge helps confirm its position.
strings.atlas.feature.3677.story: Gassendi crater on the northern edge was a finalist for Apollo 17. Scientists hoped to sample ancient rocks in its central peaks and learn the ages of the crater and Humorum basin. Rough terrain threatened access to those peaks, helping rule the site out. A scientifically promising place still had to be reachable.
strings.atlas.feature.3678.label: Mare Imbrium
strings.atlas.feature.3678.naming: Mare Imbrium means “Sea of Showers.” The Italian astronomer Giovanni Battista Riccioli named it in 1651 on a map drawn by Francesco Grimaldi. Rain, clouds and storms belong to a naming scheme shaped by the old belief that the Moon influenced weather on Earth.
strings.atlas.feature.3678.observation: Imbrium is a broad, roughly circular dark patch bordered by the bright Apennine Mountains to the southeast. That curved boundary is often easier to recognize than the small craters within it.
strings.atlas.feature.3678.story: Some isolated peaks within Imbrium are remnants of a buried mountain ring. Mons Piton still rises about 2,300 meters above the plain. It once belonged to the basin’s inner ring; later eruptions submerged most of that ring. The surviving summit reveals a landscape older than the surrounding lava.
strings.atlas.feature.3680.label: Mare Insularum
strings.atlas.feature.3680.naming: “Sea of Islands” was proposed by lunar geologist Don Wilhelms and adopted by the IAU in 1976. His first suggestion was actually Oceanus Insularum, an “Ocean of Islands,” inspired by the many highland remnants rising from the plain. The IAU kept the islands but changed the ocean to a sea. Wilhelms recounts the change in his own history of lunar exploration.
strings.atlas.feature.3680.observation: Insularum lies between Copernicus and Kepler, with scattered bright terrain interrupting its dark plains. Finding those two bright craters first can help locate the region between them.
strings.atlas.feature.3680.story: Orbital images reveal a roughly 300-meter-wide, diamond-shaped pit in Insularum. Its bowl-shaped floor holds boulders about 1 to 3 meters across. Just east of the pit, highland remnants rise above the plain: close-up examples of the “islands” recalled by the mare’s name.
strings.atlas.feature.3683.label: Mare Nectaris
strings.atlas.feature.3683.naming: Nectaris refers to nectar, the drink of the gods in classical literature. Riccioli placed this “Sea of Nectar” on the 1651 map. It joins Serenity and Tranquility in an eastern group of pleasing names, carrying an image from mythology onto another world.
strings.atlas.feature.3683.observation: South of Tranquillitatis, Nectaris is a smaller, rounded dark patch framed by bright, heavily cratered highlands. Its compact outline helps distinguish it from its larger neighbors.
strings.atlas.feature.3683.story: The visible dark patch occupies only the deep center of the Nectaris basin. Farther southwest, the curved Altai scarp traces part of its much larger ring structure. The dark plain and the distant cliff belong to the same basin, so the mare’s outline understates the scale of the impact.
strings.atlas.feature.3684.label: Mare Nubium
strings.atlas.feature.3684.naming: Nubium means “of clouds.” Riccioli named the “Sea of Clouds” in 1651, within the same weather vocabulary as the seas of rain and storms. The words preserve an old belief in the Moon’s influence on earthly weather, a connection that helped shape the names on early lunar maps.
strings.atlas.feature.3684.observation: Nubium lies in the southern half of the near side, east of Humorum. Bright terrain interrupts its edges, so look for the overall irregular outline rather than a complete circle.
strings.atlas.feature.3684.story: Near Nubium’s eastern side, the Straight Wall is a fault about 110 kilometers long with a height difference of roughly 200–300 meters. Its striking line marks displaced ground. Low sunlight emphasizes the relief, making this a useful reminder that shadows can reveal structure better than surface color.
strings.atlas.feature.3686.label: Mare Serenitatis
strings.atlas.feature.3686.naming: Serenitatis means serenity, giving this region the name “Sea of Serenity.” Riccioli named it in 1651, pairing a tranquil state of mind with a place on the Moon. The neighboring “Sea of Tranquility” is a separate feature: their similar names have shared the lunar map for centuries.
strings.atlas.feature.3686.observation: Serenitatis has a rounded outline and joins the less regular Mare Tranquillitatis to the southeast. Recognizing this pair of neighboring dark areas helps locate it.
strings.atlas.feature.3686.story: Serenitatis and neighboring Tranquillitatis differ in more than outline. Galileo spacecraft images show that Tranquillitatis contains more titanium. When colors are enhanced to reveal composition, it looks bluer. These subtle color differences help scientists map variations in lunar soil.
strings.atlas.feature.3691.label: Mare Tranquillitatis
strings.atlas.feature.3691.naming: The “Sea of Tranquility” received its name from Riccioli in 1651, more than three centuries before Apollo 11. It was already labeled on the map drawn by Grimaldi. The International Astronomical Union formally adopted the existing name in 1935, preserving a poetic choice from early lunar cartography.
strings.atlas.feature.3691.observation: Southeast of Serenitatis, Tranquillitatis spreads into a more irregular outline. Together, the two connected dark areas form a distinctive pattern on the lunar near side.
strings.atlas.feature.3691.story: On July 20, 1969, Armstrong and Aldrin landed here in Eagle. The final descent required Armstrong to steer past a crater and its scattered boulders toward safer ground. Humanity’s first lunar landing took place within the dark patch you can recognize from Earth, but its small hazards needed a much closer view.
strings.atlas.feature.3694.label: Mare Vaporum
strings.atlas.feature.3694.naming: Mare Vaporum means “Sea of Vapors.” Giovanni Battista Riccioli published the name on his 1651 lunar map, drawn by Francesco Grimaldi. It belongs to the same weather vocabulary as the seas of clouds and rain. The name survives from an era when astronomers mapped the Moon through telescopes, centuries before spacecraft could examine the surface closely.
strings.atlas.feature.3694.observation: Near the center of the near side, Vaporum lies southwest of Serenitatis and south of the Apennines. Use those larger landmarks to locate this small dark patch enclosed by brighter terrain.
strings.atlas.feature.3694.story: The apparently flat sea has a volcanic dome in its northern part. LRO photographed it from different viewpoints to produce a stereo view. Seeing the same ground from two angles reveals the dome’s shape, adding a sense of height to the familiar pattern of light and dark.
strings.atlas.feature.380.label: Aristarchus
strings.atlas.feature.380.naming: Riccioli named this crater in 1651 for Aristarchus, the ancient Greek astronomer from Samos. Long before Copernicus, Aristarchus proposed that Earth orbits the Sun. He also used the right triangle formed by Earth, Moon and Sun at half Moon to estimate their relative distances. Limited measurements kept his numerical result from being accurate.
strings.atlas.feature.380.observation: Against the dark background of Procellarum, Aristarchus often appears as a striking bright spot. It is among the Moon’s most reflective features, so the contrast can help locate it even when its rim is unclear.
strings.atlas.feature.380.story: Aristarchus stands on a plateau covered by extensive material from explosive volcanic eruptions. Nearby Vallis Schröteri is the Moon’s largest sinuous rille. The region brings together a bright impact crater and traces of a very different process: ancient volcanism.
strings.atlas.feature.4003.label: Lunar Alps
strings.atlas.feature.4003.naming: The lunar Alps take their name from the Alps on Earth. The name survives from Hevelius’s Selenographia of 1647, which filled the lunar map with familiar terrestrial geography. Most of that scheme was replaced, but Alps remained as a small part of an early way of mapping another world.
strings.atlas.feature.4003.observation: The lunar Alps stand on Imbrium’s northeastern edge, near Plato. Their bright, rough terrain borders the smooth dark plain, with low-sun shadows helping reveal the outline.
strings.atlas.feature.4003.story: The Alpine Valley contains a second, much narrower channel: a sinuous rille more than 150 kilometers long within its lava-flooded floor. Orbital images show places where lava ponded behind a constriction and then breached it, leaving a volcanic record inside the larger valley.
strings.atlas.feature.4004.label: Apennine Mountains
strings.atlas.feature.4004.naming: The lunar Apennines borrow the name of the mountain range in Italy. The name traces back to Hevelius’s 1647 Selenographia, which used terrestrial geography to label the Moon. Most of his proposed names fell out of use; Apennines is one of the few that survived into modern lunar maps.
strings.atlas.feature.4004.observation: The Apennines trace a bright arc along Imbrium’s southeastern edge. Near the lunar day–night boundary, shadows from the peaks make that border look especially rugged.
strings.atlas.feature.4004.story: In 1971, Apollo 15 explored at the foot of these mountains with the first crewed lunar rover. Scott and Irwin used it for three trips, reaching sites farther from the lander to investigate the meeting of mountain front, plain and Hadley Rille.
strings.atlas.feature.4395.label: Oceanus Procellarum
strings.atlas.feature.4395.naming: Oceanus Procellarum means “Ocean of Storms,” a name Riccioli published in 1651. He placed craters named for Copernicus and other supporters of a Sun-centered cosmos in this region, joking that he had thrown them into the storms. The map preserves a trace of the astronomical debates of its time.
strings.atlas.feature.4395.observation: Procellarum spreads across the western near side and is the largest lunar mare region. Its broad, irregular boundary cannot be reduced to a single dark oval like Crisium.
strings.atlas.feature.4395.story: Chang’e 5 brought back samples from northern Procellarum in 2020. Dating the basalt showed that lava was still erupting here about 2 billion years ago. Earlier returned samples had not documented volcanism this young, so these small pieces of rock extended the known history of lunar volcanic activity.
strings.atlas.feature.4757.label: Plato
strings.atlas.feature.4757.naming: Riccioli named this crater in 1651 for Plato, the ancient Greek philosopher whose students included Aristotle. Philosophers had a place on his Moon map alongside astronomers: he divided the surface into regions associated with thinkers from different periods and traditions.
strings.atlas.feature.4757.observation: On Imbrium’s northern edge, Plato has a dark interior bordered by brighter terrain. Its northerly location makes it appear as a dark oval with a bright rim when viewed from Earth.
strings.atlas.feature.4757.story: Plato’s smooth floor makes a useful screen for changing shadows. Ancient lava flooded the crater interior. Around local sunrise, long shadows from peaks on the eastern rim stretch across that floor while sunlight catches the raised western rim. The same crater can look very different under different lighting.
strings.atlas.feature.5565.label: Sinus Iridum
strings.atlas.feature.5565.naming: Sinus Iridum means “Bay of Rainbows.” Riccioli’s 1651 naming table gives this name alongside two earlier alternatives: van Langren’s “Bay of Geometry” and Hevelius’s “Bay of Apollo.” The three names invoke weather, mathematics, and a classical god. “Bay of Rainbows” is the one that became part of today’s official lunar map.
strings.atlas.feature.5565.observation: On Imbrium’s northwestern edge, Iridum forms a curved mountain border opening toward the plain. Low sunlight makes the bright arc and its neighboring shadows especially distinctive.
strings.atlas.feature.5565.story: The bright arc is part of an impact crater’s wall, now called the Jura Mountains. At the arc’s southern end, Cape Heraclides inspired another interpretation: Cassini’s 1679 lunar drawing depicted it as a woman’s profile with long flowing hair. The same headland can be a geological boundary or a figure in a historical map.
strings.atlas.feature.6163.label: Tycho
strings.atlas.feature.6163.naming: The crater honors Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe. Riccioli placed his name on the Moon in 1651. Tycho made exceptionally precise measurements of planetary positions without a telescope; Kepler later used his Mars observations to work out how planets move. Their names now mark two different lunar craters.
strings.atlas.feature.6163.observation: Near full Moon, look for long bright rays spreading across the southern surface, then trace them back toward Tycho. The rays are often easier to recognize than the crater itself.
strings.atlas.feature.6163.story: Tycho’s often-cited age of about 108 million years comes with a condition. Impact glass collected at the Apollo 17 landing site is thought to have been ejected from Tycho. If that origin is correct, the glass dates the crater. Samples collected inside Tycho would help test the connection.
